variables.label: Same-week savings offer
variables.guidance: 5%, set company-wide 2026-08-08 (Jack). Introduced once, after the price lands. No fixed week boundary -- deliberately left undefined (Jack, 2026-08-09): never state a specific day or timestamp to the customer, the rep uses judgment on how to describe the window (e.g. "sign this week").

variables.label: Their Accomplish List
variables.guidance: Filled per appointment. Confirmed with the homeowner at e10 before any product is presented. Phrase as outcomes in their words, never product names.

variables.label: Rep personal story (why you work here)
variables.guidance: Editable per rep on e02. Where you came from, why you chose ATH, what you think of the people you work with. Under 60 seconds. Must be true.

variables.label: Current install lead time — screens (weeks)
variables.guidance: Six to eight weeks for all screen projects. Enter as a range only -- the script supplies the word "weeks" around the token. Awnings run a different figure and now have their own key (LEAD_TIME_WEEKS_AWNINGS); the two were one shared key until this rebuild, which could never be right for both products at once.

slides.title: Table Recap on the iPad
slides.subtitle: Confirm the Scope Before You Sell Anything
purpose: Confirm you and the homeowner are looking at the same project
Surfaces install realities early, when they're a design conversation and not a surprise
slides.tone_mood: Businesslike and unhurried. This is the one part of the appointment where the rep sounds like a tradesman rather than a presenter. Reading measurements back is not exciting and it isn't supposed to be. It's the moment the homeowner decides you're competent.

blocks.label: Re-open the conversation
script: "Before I show you anything — you all said you've been in the home about [X] years, is that right?
And this space back here, is this where you spend most of your time outside, or is it more where you'd like to be spending it?"
(Let them answer. This is a genuine question and the answer usually adds an Accomplish List item.)
"Is this something you've been thinking about for a while?"

blocks.label: Recap the openings
script: "So let me walk you through what I measured, and you tell me if I've got it right.
You've got [X] openings back here. The main one across the back is [X] feet wide with about a [X] foot drop. The one on the [side] is [X] by [X].
Every screen is built to the exact opening, so those numbers are what we order to. Nothing gets cut down on site."

blocks.label: Mount type and track surface
script: "For mounting, we'd be going [surface mount / inside mount] here, attaching into [wood framing / stucco / brick / pergola posts].

The part that matters most on a screen system is that the tracks are perfectly level and perfectly parallel to each other. If they're off even a little, the screen binds. That's why we take our time here and why we don't hand this to just anybody."

blocks.label: Power
script: "These run on standard 110-volt power, so we'd plan to pull from [this outlet]. No panel work, no electrician in most cases.
We run the wire as discreetly as we can — down a post, along the trim, tucked into the soffit. If you've got paint on hand we can match it, or we can use one of the standard cover colors."
(Stage direction: point at the actual outlet and the actual wire path. Do not describe it abstractly.)

blocks.label: Sun and orientation
script: "Based on the way this faces — [west/south/east/north] — the sun is going to be hardest on you roughly [X] to [X]. That lines up with what you told me earlier about [their words].
When the screen is down during those hours, that's the difference between sitting out here and going back inside."

blocks.label: Get the yes
script: "Based on everything I just walked through — does this feel like the right approach for your space?"
👉 You need a yes here. If you get a maybe, stop and find out why. Something is unresolved and it will cost you at the close.

blocks.label: Step out
script: "Great. I'm going to pop out to the truck and grab a few samples. While I'm out there I'll start putting your numbers together. Should I let myself back in, or would you rather I knock?"
(Update the sales form and prepare the estimates outside. Do not transcribe onto paper yet — that happens at the table.)

display_beats: How long in the home · is this where you spend time
Recap every opening: width × drop
Mount type and what we're attaching to
Tracks must be level and parallel — say why
110V, show the actual outlet and wire path
Sun orientation vs. their stated problem
Get the yes
Step outside for samples and numbers

slow_down_on.line: If they're off even a little, the screen binds.
slow_down_on.why: this is the entire justification for your install premium, delivered before price exists. It's a mechanical fact, not a sales claim, which is exactly why it lands.

slides.coaching_note:
New reps skip this block because it feels like housekeeping and they're eager to get to the product. It is the opposite of housekeeping. Every install surprise you don't surface here becomes a change order, a bad review, or a lost sale later. The homeowner who watches you point at their actual outlet and their actual soffit has already decided you've done this before.

Never recap measurements from memory. Have them on the screen. Reading them off confidently and being slightly boring here buys you enormous credibility for the next thirty minutes.

engagement_question.text: Is this where you spend most of your time outside, or where you'd like to be?
branches: the second half of that question is what produces Accomplish List gold. Most people answer the second half.

slides.title: Pre-Frame
slides.subtitle: Set Expectations and Take the Room
purpose: Position yourself as the guide, not a presenter
Introduce the two-option structure now so pricing later feels expected
slides.tone_mood: Friendly and confident. Sitting, not standing. Relaxed body language. This is forty-five seconds of warmth before any content — the rep should sound like a guest who's glad to be there, because he is.

script: "Well — thanks again for having me out. Not everybody offers us water and puts up with us tracking through the yard, so I appreciate that.

Here's what I'd like to do. Take about fifteen minutes, walk you through how these screen systems actually work, what makes them different from the other things out there, and how we'd design this specifically for your space.
Then we'll look at a couple of options together and figure out what actually makes sense for you. Sound good?"
(Get the yes.)

display_beats: Thank them, be human for ten seconds
Fifteen minutes, here's what we'll cover
Two options at the end — plant it now
"Sound good?" — get the yes

slow_down_on.line: figure out what actually makes sense for you.
slow_down_on.why: it's the sentence that separates a consultation from a pitch, and it's the frame you'll lean on at every objection later.

slides.coaching_note:
Reps who skip the pre-frame end up fighting for control of the appointment for the next half hour. Forty-five seconds of "here's what's about to happen" means the homeowner stops wondering when the sales part starts, because you already told them.

Say "a couple of options" out loud here. When two options appear at pricing, they'll feel like the plan instead of a tactic.

slides.title: Eclipse® E-Zip Motorized Screens
purpose: Re-anchor the conversation on their problem, in their words
Last chance to add to the Accomplish List before the presentation starts
slides.tone_mood: Conversational and curious. The rep is asking, not telling. If the homeowner isn't doing most of the talking during this slide, it's being run wrong.

blocks.label: The frustration question
script: "Before we jump in — when you're out here trying to enjoy this space, what's the thing that pushes you back inside most often?"
(Let them answer. Do not fill the silence. Listen for sun angle, wind, heat, bugs, or privacy.)
"And what time of day is it usually the worst?"
(West-facing: afternoon. South: midday. East: morning. North: usually wind or privacy.)

blocks.label: Frame the goal
script: "So really, the whole goal here is to make this space usable on your terms — when you want to be out here — without fighting the elements every single time.
That's exactly what we're going to walk through."

slides.transition_out: Let me start with who we are, because honestly, who installs this matters just as much as what gets installed.
display_beats: "What pushes you back inside most often?" — then stop talking
"What time of day is worst?" — anchors sun angle
Reflect it back: usable on your terms, without fighting the elements
Add anything new to the Accomplish List right now

slow_down_on.line: on your terms.
slow_down_on.why: control is what this product actually sells. Not shade — control. Plant the word early and it pays off at the money slide when you explain the screen stops at any height.

slides.coaching_note:
Two to three minutes here anchors everything that follows. The clearer the pain, the easier the close. Reps rush this because it feels like they're not doing anything, but the homeowner describing their own problem out loud is worth more than any slide you'll show them.

Write down their exact words. Not your translation of their words. "The wind flat out ruins dinner out here" is worth ten times "wind mitigation" when you say it back at pricing.

engagement_question.text: What sort of things do you all like to do out here?
engagement_question.when: use it if the first question produces a short answer
branches: Follow with: dinner? drinks? grandkids? Something always comes loose.

slides.title: Who We Are — Local & Family-Owned
purpose: Trust and local positioning — the first credibility slide, before any product talk
Homeowners buy the rep before they buy the company
slides.tone_mood: Warm, grounded, unhurried. Neighbor, not presenter. No selling energy yet. Roughly half this slide is the rep's personal story and that half should not be rushed.

blocks.label: The company
script: "Quick background on us.

We're Around The House Home Solutions. Local, family-owned, based right up in Monument. We've been in business since 2004, so twenty-two years now, and in that time we've completed thousands of projects across the Front Range. Over four thousand customers. This isn't something we picked up last year.
Our focus is the exterior of the home — high quality shade and protection solutions, so people can actually enjoy living in Colorado instead of hiding from it.
Something our customers really appreciate — we're not a big corporation out of Denver. You call us, you get us."

blocks.label: Personal touch (editable per rep)
script: {{REP_PERSONAL_STORY}}
blocks.sample: Sample — Matt: "Myself, I've been in home remodeling since I graduated college in 2014. I've worked for everything from big national remodeling companies to small owner-operated contractors — full home additions, interior remodels, decks, concrete patios. Somewhere along the way I figured out I have to actually like where I work. So when I met Jack and his brother Maxx, and saw how they treat customers and each other, I couldn't pass it up. I'm really happy I found my home here."

slides.transition_out: Outside of screens, we handle a few other things around the house too.
display_beats: Local, family-owned, Monument
Since 2004 — twenty-two years, thousands of projects, 4,000+ customers
Exterior focus — enjoy Colorado, don't hide from it
Not a Denver corporation: you call us, you get us
YOUR personal story

slow_down_on.line: You call us, you get us.
slow_down_on.why: it's the whole slide in five words. Say it, stop, let it land.

slides.coaching_note:
The personal touch is not filler and it is not optional. Homeowners buy the rep before they buy the company. A new rep who skips it because it feels self-indulgent will feel the difference at the close.

Write your own version. Same shape as Matt's: where you came from, why you chose here, what you think of the people you work with. Under sixty seconds, and make it true. A story you're embarrassed to tell is worse than no story.

slides.title: Your Home Solutions Experts
purpose: Establish ATH as a full exterior company, not a one-product screen outfit
Opens the cross-sell door without forcing it
slides.tone_mood: Confident and moving. The one slide where the rep is allowed to sound like he's covering ground. Breadth is the point; depth belongs to the screens.

script: "So a lot of homeowners don't realize the full picture of what we do.

We've been the authorized dealer for Gutter Helmet and heat cable systems for all twenty-two years we've been in business — that's a patented gutter and roof protection system, so you never clean your gutters again. Keeps people off ladders and protects the exterior of the home.
Sunesta retractable awnings for overhead shade — we're actually Sunesta's Dealer of the Year.

Motorized louvered roof systems, attached and freestanding. Commercial grade, built for the wind we get out here. A lot of our customers pair those with screens to create a real three-season outdoor room.
And of course the motorized screens, which is what we're here for today.
Everything's made in the USA and most of it carries a lifetime warranty."

slides.transition_out: Outside of family, your home is usually the biggest investment you've got. So we only install products we'd put on our own houses, and we install them to a standard we can stand behind.
display_beats: Gutter Helmet — 22 years, never clean your gutters again
Sunesta awnings — Dealer of the Year
Louvered roofs — commercial grade, pairs with screens
Motorized screens — today's focus
Made in USA, mostly lifetime warranties
Offer to measure anything else — then move on

slow_down_on.line: all twenty-two years we've been in business.
slow_down_on.why: longevity is the proof point on this slide. Say the number, pause a beat, move on.

slides.coaching_note: The offer to look at other products is a seed, not an invitation. If the homeowner bites — "actually, what would a louvered roof run?" — acknowledge it and park it: "Great question, let's absolutely look at that. Let me finish walking you through the screens first and we'll come back to it." Chasing a second product mid-presentation doubles the length and usually costs you both sales. Plant it here, harvest it after the close.
callback_triggers: Homeowner mentions a pergola or louvered roof later
Homeowner asks about gutters, ice, or roof runoff
At the close, if a second product came up and you parked it

slides.title: Installed In-House — Level, Parallel, To the Inch
purpose: Differentiate install quality — this is the slide that justifies price before price exists
Screens are less forgiving than almost anything else we install, and that's the whole argument
slides.tone_mood: Calm authority. Not defensive, not bitter about competitors. The rep is describing how a professional does it and letting the contrast speak. Slight smile on the "chuck in a truck" line so it lands as observation rather than attack.

blocks.label: Why install matters more here
script: "This is worth a minute before we get to the product.

You can buy a great screen system and still end up unhappy, because a screen is less forgiving than almost anything else we install. The two side tracks have to be perfectly level and perfectly parallel to each other. Not close — parallel. If they're off, the fabric binds, the motor works against itself, and eventually something gives.
It's not like hanging a curtain. There's real precision to it."

blocks.label: Who does the work
script: "Our install teams work exclusively for us. Same crews that do our awnings and our louvered roofs — they're trained by us, they know these systems, and we inspect and warranty every job.

A lot of companies out there, it's more of a 'chuck in a truck' situation. They'll install four or five of these a year, so they slap it up and hope for the best. There's no consistency from one job to the next, and that's how homeowners end up paying for the same project twice."
(Slight smile on "chuck in a truck." Let it land as a joke about the industry, not a specific competitor.)

blocks.label: Licensing and accountability
script: "Most shade products in Colorado don't require a permit, which keeps the barrier to entry very low for inexperienced companies. Because we also do larger structures like pergolas, we hold our PPRBD license in good standing and we build to code regardless of project size.
We're licensed and insured, so if something happens on the job, you're protected and we're protected.
And we do a final walkthrough on every install. If anything ever comes up, you call our 719 number and we come out. That's it."

slides.transition_out: So that's us. Let me tell you about the people who'll actually be at your house.
display_beats: Screens are unforgiving — tracks must be level AND parallel
Off by a little = binding, motor strain, failure
Our teams, exclusively ours, trained by us
"Chuck in a truck" — light delivery
No permit required in CO = low barrier for bad companies
PPRBD licensed, insured, build to code anyway
Final walkthrough, one number to call

slow_down_on.line: Not close — parallel.
slow_down_on.why: it's the most specific, most technical, most credible thing on the slide, and it's completely verifiable. A homeowner who understands why precision matters has a reason to distrust a cheap bid that they came up with themselves.

slides.coaching_note:
This is the highest-leverage trust slide in the deck and the easiest one to rush, because it's all company talk and no product. Don't. Every dollar of difference between your number and a cheaper bid gets defended right here. Skip it and the price objection arrives later with nothing to push back against.

Deliver "chuck in a truck" lightly. The moment it sounds like you're running down competitors, the homeowner starts defending them.

engagement_question.text: Have you had work done on the home before? How was that experience?
branches: If good: agree, be glad for them, move on.
If bad: this industry is notorious for it, and communication and timelines are what people complain about most, which is exactly why we run it the way we do.

reactive_scripts.question: Do you use subcontractors?
answer: "Our crew is 1099 technicians. But our install teams work exclusively for us — they're trained by us, we inspect every job, and we warranty every job. And our production and quality assurance guys are full-time employees.
So the accountability doesn't move. It's us either way."
reactive_scripts.note: Never volunteer this. Do not say "we don't use subcontractors" and do not bring the word into the room. If asked, answer plainly and move on. The honesty is the point — a rep who dodges this question loses more than one who answers it.

slides.title: Our People — Who Actually Shows Up
purpose: Answer the question every homeowner has and almost none of them ask
Hands the homeowner a framework they'll use to evaluate the next bid they get
slides.tone_mood: Steady and matter-of-fact. Not proud, not pitching. The rep is answering a fair question directly, which is itself the persuasive part.

blocks.label: The pivot
script: "You can build a great company and a great process, but if you don't have the right people on a project, it doesn't go well. So when people are vetting a contractor, it really comes down to three questions."

blocks.label: The three questions
script: "How long have they been doing this? We've been at it twenty-two years and installed thousands of projects across the Front Range. That takes a lot of people management to get right.
Who's actually performing the work? Our own certified technicians, a fully staffed operations department, and install teams who work with us and only us.

Are they qualified? Our teams are trained to Eclipse's specification and to our own standards on top of that — and ours are higher. We do that because we want your screens to look right on day one and still look right in fifteen years.
And behind all of it there's an operations team on every project, so you're not depending on me to remember to follow up."

slides.transition_out: That's who we are. Let me tell you who builds the product.
display_beats: Great company + wrong people = bad project
Three questions: how long · who does the work · are they qualified
22 years, thousands of projects
Our technicians, our ops team, our install crews
Trained to Eclipse spec AND our standards — ours are higher
Ops team on every project — not depending on me to follow up

slow_down_on.line: you're not depending on me to remember to follow up.
slow_down_on.why: it's disarmingly honest and it's the fear behind every one-truck operation. Say it plainly.

slides.coaching_note:
The three questions do quiet competitive work. A cheaper bidder usually can't answer any of them well, and you've just handed the homeowner a framework to evaluate that bid with. They'll use it whether you're in the room or not.

Don't oversell this slide. It's a straight answer to a fair question and it's most persuasive when it sounds like one.

slides.title: Eclipse® Authorized Dealer
purpose: Establish the manufacturer as a real company that will still exist in fifteen years
Answers the unspoken fear behind every cheap bid — an orphaned warranty
slides.tone_mood: Steady and factual. This is a heritage slide, so let the dates and the places do the work. The rep should sound like he finds this genuinely interesting, not like he's reciting a brochure.

blocks.label: Who builds it
script: "So that's us. Let me tell you who actually builds the product.

Eclipse Shading Systems is out of Middletown, New York, with additional manufacturing down in Statesville, North Carolina. They've been building the E-Zip side-retention system since 2002, and the larger seven-inch line since 2019.
Everything is custom made in the USA, built to the inch for your specific opening. There's nothing off the shelf in this."

blocks.label: Why the manufacturer matters
script: "Here's why I bring that up.
When you buy something like this, you're really trusting two companies. The one who installs it and the one who builds it. If either one disappears, your warranty goes with them.

A lot of the cheaper systems out there are assembled from parts sourced from three or four different suppliers. Nobody owns the whole thing. When something fails in year six, you're chasing a component manufacturer overseas.
With this, it's one product family from one manufacturer, and we're the licensed and insured authorized dealer for it right here. Two companies, both accountable, both still going to be here."

slides.transition_out: Let me show you what that actually gets you.
display_beats: Middletown NY, manufacturing in Statesville NC
E-Zip since 2002 · 7-inch since 2019
Custom made in the USA, built to the inch
You're trusting two companies — installer and manufacturer
Cheap systems = parts from four suppliers, nobody owns it
One product family, one manufacturer, licensed local dealer

slow_down_on.line: If either one disappears, your warranty goes with them.
slow_down_on.why: it's the real fear behind a low bid and it's the one thing a cheap competitor genuinely cannot answer. Say it plainly, don't oversell it, move on.

slides.coaching_note:
Homeowners worry about two failures — the product breaking, and the company vanishing. Slides 2 through 5 answered the second one about ATH. This slide answers it about Eclipse, and it matters more than reps think.

Say the specific places out loud. "Middletown, New York" and "Statesville, North Carolina" sound like real towns where real people build things. "American-made" by itself sounds like marketing.

Do not turn this into a product slide. The product gets sold in Tab 3. This slide's only job is making the manufacturer feel permanent.

slides.title: Why Eclipse
purpose: Stack proof fast — engineering, motor, fabric, wind
Every badge needs a "which means" or it's decoration
slides.tone_mood: Brisk and confident. This is a stack, so keep it moving — one item, one sentence of meaning, next. The one place to slow down is wind, because that's the item tied to something the homeowner has personally watched happen in their own backyard.

blocks.label: The product line
script: "A few things worth knowing about what you're actually getting.

Eclipse has been building this exact system since 2002 — residential and commercial, all over the country. It's a refined product at this point, not a first attempt. One consistent product family, custom made to the inch."

blocks.label: The motor
script: "The motor is Somfy, and it comes standard. Same brand used in premium motorized systems worldwide. That's not a small thing — the motor is the part that has to work ten thousand times without you thinking about it.
Handheld remote, wireless wall switch, or your phone. And it'll integrate with home automation if you ever want to go that direction."

blocks.label: The fabric
script: "The fabric is Phifer SunTex. Phifer is one of the most respected shading fabric manufacturers in the world, and SunTex is GREENGUARD Gold certified — which means it's been independently tested for what it off-gasses, and it passed the strictest tier.
On top of the Eclipse warranty, Phifer backs the fabric with their own ten-year exterior warranty. So the fabric has two companies behind it too."

blocks.label: Wind
script: "And this is the one that matters most out here.
The four and five inch systems carry a Class 6 wind rating, tested to eighty miles per hour, and they carry Miami-Dade County approval — that's the hurricane standard."
(Localize. Use their house.)
"You mentioned the wind rips through here in the afternoon — that's exactly what that rating is about.
What makes it work is the zipper retention. The fabric edge is physically locked into the side track, so instead of billowing and flapping like a generic roll-down screen, it stays flat and taut."

slides.transition_out: Let me show you some of these in the wild.
display_beats: E-Zip since 2002 — refined, not a first attempt
Somfy motor STANDARD — the part that has to work 10,000 times
Phifer SunTex, GREENGUARD Gold — plus Phifer's own 10-year fabric warranty
Class 6, 80 MPH, Miami-Dade approval
LOCALIZE the wind line to their house, every time
Zipper retention = flat and taut, not flapping

slow_down_on.line: the wind localization
slow_down_on.why: this is the moment an engineering number becomes a thing the homeowner has watched happen on their own patio. A rep who reads "Class 6, 80 MPH" and moves on has wasted the strongest item on the slide.

slides.coaching_note:
Every badge needs a "which means" attached to it. Miami-Dade means nothing to a Colorado homeowner until you say hurricane standard. GREENGUARD Gold means nothing until you say independently tested and passed the strictest tier. A new rep reads the badge and moves on — the translation is the entire job of this slide.

Keep it moving otherwise. Four items in two minutes means roughly thirty seconds each. If you're still on the motor at the ninety second mark, you're going to lose the room before you get to wind, which is the one they actually care about.

reactive_scripts.question: Only if they ask about reviews or ratings

I'd say that's per Eclipse's published reviews rather than something I can independently verify, but it's consistent with what we see."

slides.title: Real Projects — Right Here on the Front Range
purpose: Localization equals credibility — closes "have you done work around here?" before it's asked
Proof that their exact problem has already been solved for someone nearby
slides.tone_mood: Relaxed and specific. This is show-and-tell, not a pitch. Slow the pace — photos are one of the few moments a homeowner is genuinely looking at the screen instead of at the rep.

script: "These are all local. Every one of these is a project we've done on the Front Range."
(Point to the photo closest to their situation.)
"This one here is very similar to what you've got — same exposure, same kind of opening, same problem with the afternoon sun.
Here's what it looks like with the screens up. You barely notice it's there. Clean cassette, low profile, looks like it was designed with the house.
And here's the same space with them down."
(On multi-opening projects.)
"This one's a full enclosure — multiple screens across multiple openings. That homeowner basically turned their patio into an outdoor room. They use it most of the year now."

slides.transition_out: And it's not just a handful of projects — let me show you where these are.
display_beats: Every photo is local — say it
Point to the ONE closest to their situation and say why
Up: barely visible, looks designed-in
Down: the space is transformed
Multi-opening: outdoor room, used most of the year

slow_down_on.line: the tie-back to their situation
slow_down_on.why: don't say it while advancing the slide. Say it, stop, and let them look at the photo while the comparison sinks in.

slides.coaching_note:
The whole value of this slide is that it's their neighborhood and their problem on somebody else's house. A generic "here are some installs" wastes it.

Before the appointment, pick the two photos closest to this customer — same exposure, same deck style, same part of town. If you can name the general area and they recognize it, that's worth more than any badge in the deck.

slides.title: We've Worked in Your Neighborhood
purpose: Turn "have you done work around here?" into a visual answer
Sets up an asset you'll return to during price conditioning
slides.tone_mood: Easy and conversational. The map does the talking. Let the homeowner look for their own street — that's the moment that lands, and it only happens if the rep stops talking.

script: "We've completed projects all over the greater Colorado Springs area — Monument, Falcon, Black Forest, the Springs, out toward Peyton.
Every home is a little different, but at this point we've worked through just about every scenario there is."

blocks.label: Top to bottom
script: "Here's the whole system, without getting into the weeds.

script: (Hand them the cassette sample.)
"Feel that. That's two-piece powder-coated extruded aluminum. Every size, same construction.
The reason I hand you that is a lot of cheaper systems use roll-form housing, which is basically painted sheet metal bent into a shape. This is structurally a different thing.
And inside it is the largest roller tube that'll fit that cassette. A bigger tube resists sag, which means your fabric hangs flat and stays flat — not just this year, in ten years."

blocks.label: Standard vs Super Duty
script: (Hand them both track sections. Standard first, then Super Duty. Let them feel the difference before you explain it.)
"Now here's the actual choice.
Both versions carry the same warranty — lifetime on the frame, the fabric, the motor, and the electronics. That doesn't change either way you go.

(Point at the two samples in their hands.)
"You can feel it — the Standard track holds the fabric edge. The Super Duty track holds it and keeps tension on it under load. The hem bar's heavier too, with an internal steel channel.

But they're built for coastal storm zones, and you pay for that. In Monument you're solving for afternoon wind and sun, not a hurricane. That's genuine overkill for what you're dealing with."

blocks.label: Doing nothing
script: "And of course you could do nothing. Which is a real option. It just means next summer looks like this one."

slides.transition_out: So that's the landscape. Let me show you where the money actually falls.
display_beats: Generic rollers: no zipper, held top and bottom only, fails in our wind
Glass sunroom: $50,000+, permanent, traps heat, can't open it
DIY sails/umbrellas: one season, no wind protection, stopgap
MagnaTrack-class: 150+ MPH, real product, built for hurricanes — overkill here
Do nothing: next summer looks like this one
Even tone throughout. No sneering.

slow_down_on.line: In Monument you're solving for afternoon wind and sun, not a hurricane.
slow_down_on.why: it's the line that makes ATH the sensible middle instead of the expensive option. You just told them not to overbuy, which is the most credible thing a salesperson can say.

slides.coaching_note:
Naming a real competitor product honestly — MagnaTrack is good, it's just built for a different problem — buys you enormous credibility. A rep who claims every alternative is garbage sounds like a salesman. A rep who says one of them is excellent and wrong for this house sounds like an advisor.

Only bring up glass sunrooms if they're actually in play or the homeowner raises them. Don't hand someone a new idea to go price out.

slides.title: Not All Shade Costs the Same
purpose: Price conditioning — build the range before revealing their number
Turns "how much is it?" from a fear into a question they already know the answer to
slides.tone_mood: Loosest the rep has been since the fabric slide. A little funny, genuinely helpful. Energy comes back up here on purpose, because the last two slides were serious. By the end of this slide the room should feel easier, not tighter.

blocks.label: Set it up
script: "Alright. Before I show you numbers, let me give you some context, because 'patio screen' can mean about five completely different things depending on who you're talking to.
I'd rather you know where everything falls than have me throw a number at you cold."

blocks.label: The bottom
script: "At the very bottom you've got the DIY stuff. Roll-up bamboo, a sail, an outdoor curtain off a website. Five hundred to a thousand dollars, and honestly? For a summer or two, fine.

Then the low-end installed screens. Somewhere around a thousand to three thousand an opening. Manual usually, no zipper track, minimal warranty — a year on components if you're lucky. Somebody hangs it and moves on."
(Light delivery here.)
"The problem isn't really the screen. It's that when something goes wrong there's nobody to call. And if it's motorized at that price, the motor is the part that goes first."

blocks.label: The top
script: "On the other end, the hurricane-rated systems and the glass enclosures. MagnaTrack-class screens, full sunrooms — you're talking twenty thousand on the low end and it runs to a hundred thousand plus for a real glass room.
Beautiful, seriously engineered, and built for a problem you don't have."

blocks.label: Where we live
script: "A quality motorized screen — real zipper retention, name-brand fabric, a real company, a real warranty, professionally installed — is going to land somewhere between four thousand and twelve thousand depending on how many openings and how big they are.

We're going to fall right in there. We're not the cheapest quote you'll get, and honestly I'd be a little worried if we were. But we're not the most expensive either, and there's a reason for that — we do a lot of volume with Eclipse, and that buying power comes back to you."

blocks.label: Hand off
script: "So that's the landscape. Nothing I'm about to show you should be a surprise.
And based on everything we talked about — {{ACCOMPLISH_LIST}}"
(Name their Accomplish List items.)
"— I think you're going to like where this comes in."
👉 Smile. Go straight into pricing. Do not pause for questions here.

slow_down_on.why: it's the most valuable sentence on the slide. Honest, slightly funny, and it inoculates against every competing bid they'll see for the next three weeks.

slides.coaching_note:
This slide exists so your number isn't the first piece of price information in the room. A homeowner with no reference point hears a price and reacts emotionally. A homeowner who just agreed that a quality screen runs four to twelve hears a price and evaluates it. Same number, completely different conversation.

Say the ranges with total ease. Any hesitation or apology in your voice tells them the price is high before they've heard it. Sound like a guy explaining how the market works, not a guy softening a blow.

The humor lives at the bottom of the range, not the top. Cheap screens are funny. Expensive ones need to sound serious, because their job is making our number feel reasonable.

Do not stop for questions at the end. The energy built here is what carries into the reveal. A pause lets it leak out and invites a pre-emptive objection before there's a number to object to.

slides.title: Up, It Disappears. Down, It's Protected.
purpose: Last emotional beat before numbers — leave them picturing the space, not the spec
slides.tone_mood: Warm and brief. Everything before this was information. This is a picture.

script: "That's really the whole idea.
When you don't need it, it's gone — up in the cassette, you'd barely know it's there. When you do, the sun's off you, the wind's off you, and you're still outside.
You're not giving up the space to get the protection. You're just finally in control of it."
(Pause.)
"Any questions about any of it? The product, the company, me — anything at all?"
👉 Ask it and then actually wait. This is the last clean chance to surface a concern before price is on the table.

slides.transition_out: Alright — let me show you what I put together.
display_beats: Up: gone. Down: protected. Still outside either way.
"You're not giving up the space to get the protection"
Ask the open question — then WAIT
An objection surfaced here costs far less than after a number

slow_down_on.line: You're not giving up the space to get the protection.
slow_down_on.why: it's the resolution of the fear that's been sitting underneath the whole appointment, and it's the last thing you want in their head before numbers.

slides.coaching_note: The open-questions ask is not a formality. It's the cheapest possible moment to discover an objection. New reps ask it and immediately keep talking, which defeats the entire purpose. Ask, stop, count to five in your head.

Hand them the SunTex 95 and then stop talking

Localize the wind story to their house, every time

Make a recommendation on duty level and give the reason

slides.title: Pricing & Close
slides.coaching_note: Urgency mechanic is {{SAME_WEEK_SAVINGS}} — introduced calmly, once, AFTER the price lands and is absorbed. Never lead with it, never repeat it as pressure. Rep-only; it never appears on a customer slide. Percentage is set at the company level, not by the rep.

blocks.label: The four sales you must make
script: 1. Do the project — they believe this space is worth solving for
2. Do it right — they believe the quality and warranty justify the investment
3. Do it with ATH — they trust you, the company, and the install
4. Do it now — the same-week savings and the six-to-eight-week lead time both support this
If you lose the sale, trace it back to which one wasn't closed. That's your gap.

blocks.label: Accomplish List — master E-Zip version
script: ☐ Use the space during peak sun hours, not just mornings and evenings
☐ Block the harsh sun from wherever it hits hardest
☐ Cut the wind so the space is comfortable to sit in
☐ Keep the view — see out without being blasted
☐ Reduce heat and glare reaching the rooms behind the space
☐ Add privacy from neighbors or the street
☐ Keep no-see-ums and mosquitoes out so evenings work
☐ Extend usability into more months of the year
☐ Push-button convenience
☐ Make it look finished and intentional, not pieced together
☐ Create a true outdoor room
☐ Something that holds up in Colorado wind long-term

blocks.label: Post-install — the referral program (not part of the presentation)
script: Referral program: $200 gift card once a referred project is installed.

👉 Never mentioned during the sales appointment. This is a post-install conversation, raised at the walkthrough or the twelve-month Shade Service visit. Bringing it up while selling makes the recommendation sound transactional.

reactive_scripts.question: Will I still be able to see my view?
answer: "That's the most common question we get, and it's the right one to ask. Let me show you rather than tell you."
(Hand them the SunTex 95.)

"Look through it. You keep your view — the heat and glare are gone but you're not staring at a wall. And from outside during the day it reads almost like a mirror. They can't see in, you can see out."

reactive_scripts.question: Will it hold up in Colorado wind?
answer: "That's one of the strongest things about this system. The four and five inch carry a Class 6 rating, tested to eighty, and they're Miami-Dade approved — that's the hurricane standard.
What makes it work is the zipper. The fabric edge is physically locked into the track for the whole drop, so it stays flat instead of billowing.

Eclipse also ran these in dynamic wind testing in Pennsylvania — the SunTex fabric came through with no damage at a hundred and thirty. Two competing fabrics in the same test failed at a hundred ten and seventy."
reactive_scripts.note: Frame 130 as the fabric test result. Not a system rating.

reactive_scripts.question: Is it going to feel like a cage?
answer: "It really doesn't, and that's a fair thing to wonder. Unlike a glass room, this is a screen — air moves through it, so it doesn't trap heat. You still feel like you're outside, just without the sun on you.
And it's motorized, so it's never permanent. All the way down, halfway, or completely gone in about twenty seconds."
(Go back to the Before/After/Inside slide rather than arguing.)

reactive_scripts.question: How do we get in and out?
answer: "You run it up with the remote — takes seconds. There's no door panel in this system; you enter and exit by raising the screen. Most people stop thinking about it after the first week."

reactive_scripts.question: Will it keep no-see-ums out?
answer: "Yes — the SunTex weave is tight enough for no-see-ums and mosquitoes, and the brush seal on the hem bar closes the gap at the floor. For a lot of our customers that's the thing that changed how much they use the space in the evening."

reactive_scripts.question: What about hail?
answer: "Fair question out here. Realistically, screens do well with hail because they hang vertically — hail comes down at an angle and mostly glances off rather than hitting flat. We see very little hail damage on these compared to roofs or awnings.
If something ever did happen, it'd typically be covered under your homeowner's policy the same as any other exterior damage, and we can handle minor touchups ourselves."

reactive_scripts.question: We got a quote for a lot less.
answer: "That's worth digging into, because the price gap usually comes down to three specific things.

Does their system use a true zipper retention track, or is the fabric only held top and bottom? What's the actual warranty — all four components, or split up by part with different terms? And is the fabric a name brand with published UV data?
Those three questions will tell you a lot about what you're actually comparing."

reactive_scripts.question: We want to think about it.
answer: "Totally fair. Help me understand where you're at — on a scale of one to ten, how close does this feel to being the right move?"
(7 or above: find the specific gap. Below 7: something bigger is unresolved.)
"What's the one thing that would need to be different for this to be an easy yes?"

reactive_scripts.question: We want another quote.
answer: "Completely reasonable — I'd do the same. When you're comparing, ask about the zipper track, the full warranty terms, and the fabric manufacturer. Those three will tell you most of what you need to know."

reactive_scripts.question: It's more than we expected.
answer: "I hear you. Is it the whole project, or is it the size of it?

If it's scope, we can look at doing the opening that solves the biggest problem now and holding the price on the rest for a year. If it's the system, we can talk about what Standard versus Super Duty actually means for your exposure.
We'll find the version of this that works for where you're at."
reactive_scripts.note: Remove openings the homeowner chooses. Adjust scope before discounting.

reactive_scripts.question: We need to talk it over.
answer: "Of course. Is there anything we haven't covered that would help when you walk them through it? And is there any chance we could get them on a quick call? I'd rather answer questions directly than have it go through a game of telephone."

reactive_scripts.question: We might wait until next season.
answer: "Totally your call, and I'll be straight with you on timing. We're six to eight weeks out right now because everything is built to your openings. When the warm weather hits, that stretches.
The practical piece is that every week this isn't up is another week you're not using the space. But whenever it's right for you is the right time."

reactive_scripts.question: We're thinking about a pergola or louvered roof first.
answer: "That actually makes good sense, and the two work really well together. We do the Eclipse Latitude louvered roof system as well — a lot of our customers pair the roof overhead with screens on the sides to create a true outdoor room.
If that's the direction, let's talk through both so whatever you do now sets up cleanly for what comes later."

reactive_scripts.question: Do you offer financing?
answer: "We do. Unlike credit cards with annual fees and rates up into the high twenties, we work with home improvement lenders. No prepayment penalty, and anything extra you pay goes straight to principal.

There are low monthly budget plans with rates as low as 10.99%, or a twelve-month no-interest, same-as-cash option. Both are zero money down, with the first payment not due until after the install is complete.
We can check pre-approval with no impact on your credit. Want me to look at that?"

reactive_scripts.question: Do you use subcontractors?
answer: "Our crew is 1099 technicians. But our install teams work exclusively for us — they're trained by us, we inspect every job, and we warranty every job. Our production and quality assurance guys are full-time employees.
So the accountability doesn't move. It's us either way."

reactive_scripts.question: E-Zip vs. Sunesta — rep reference
answer: Solves — Sunesta: Overhead sun. E-Zip: The whole opening — sun, wind, privacy, bugs.
Their pain — Sunesta: Can't use it midday. E-Zip: Elements push them off entirely.
Wind story — Sunesta: Arms tested to 98 MPH. E-Zip: Class 6 / 80 MPH certified · fabric tested to 130.
Differentiator — Sunesta: Smart Case. E-Zip: Zipper retention track.
Fabric choice — Sunesta: Color and pattern. E-Zip: UV blockage — 95 is almost always right.
Two options — Sunesta: Sunesta vs Sunstyle. E-Zip: Which openings now vs. later.
Common objection — Sunesta: Will it block our view? E-Zip: Will it feel like a cage?
Competitor contrast — Sunesta: Frankenstein awnings. E-Zip: Generic rollers, glass sunrooms.
Cross-sell — Sunesta: Drop screen, LED lights. E-Zip: More openings, louvered roof.

modules.title: Pricing Transition & Close
modules.tone_mood: Confident and genuinely excited — not performed. The rep should sound like someone about to hand over good news. Any hesitation, apology, or throat-clearing tells the homeowner the number is high before they've seen it. Indifference is the target: warm, engaged, completely unattached to the outcome.

phases.label: LAY OFF THE PRICE
script: "Are you all excited?"
(If rapport supports it: "Should I do a drum roll?")
"So based on everything we talked about — and your goals of {{ACCOMPLISH_LIST}} —"
(Repeat the Accomplish List. Their words.)
"— this is what I put together for you.

These numbers include the complete system on [X] openings, custom built to your exact dimensions, Somfy motorization, the SunTex fabric in the color you picked, professional installation by our team, and the Platinum Protection Plus lifetime warranty.
We're six to eight weeks out, and your install is a one-day job. And most importantly, you get this space back."

phases.label: PRESENT TWO OPTIONS
script: 👉 Primary fork is scope. Secondary fork is duty level.
"This option is designed to give you everything you said you wanted."
Option 1 — The full scope. Every opening, the recommended duty level.
Option 2 — The priority scope. The opening or openings that solve the biggest problem, with the rest priced so they can add later at today's number.
"Option one covers all [X] openings — the whole space, done at once.

Option two is if you'd rather start with the [main opening], which is where the real problem is, and add the others down the road. I've priced those out so you know exactly what they'd be whenever you're ready."
👉 If duty level is genuinely in play, present it as a line within each option rather than as a third option. Two options, never three.

phases.label: REBUILD EXCITEMENT
script: "And the good news is you caught us at a good time."
👉 First the one-year price. This is the safety net — it lowers pressure in the room.

"First thing — this price is good for a full year. You can call me tomorrow, six months from now, three hundred sixty-four days from now, and this is locked. I'm not coming back to tell you it went up. That's yours either way."
👉 Pause. Let it land. They need to feel unpressured before you give them a reason to move.
👉 Then the savings. Once, with authority. Do not repeat it, do not apologize for it.

"The one thing that doesn't hold for a year is this — we're running {{SAME_WEEK_SAVINGS}} for folks who get on the schedule this week. That's not a pressure thing, it's just how we plan the install calendar. The price is protected either way. That piece isn't."
👉 Then stop talking about it. Moving on immediately is what keeps it from feeling like a pitch.

phases.label: MICRO-CLOSE
script: "Does this all make sense so far?"
👉 Wait for the answer. This is a checkpoint, not a rhetorical question.

phases.label: CLOSE TRANSITION
script: "So between the two we've talked through — which one feels like the right starting point for you?"
👉 NOT "What do you think?" or "Any questions?"
The close is a preference question. Give them a direction to move in.
What you'll typically hear:
"Let's just do all of them — we'd rather not do this twice." (most common)
"Let's start with the back and see how we like it." (a yes, not a no — write it)
"What's the difference if we went Super Duty on the big one?" (a buying question — answer it and close)

phases.label: RIGHT-SIZING ORDER OF OPERATIONS
script: If the number needs to come down, in this order:
1. Remove openings. Let them choose which. Hold the price on the rest for a year.
2. Step down duty level where exposure genuinely allows it.
3. Downgrade the warranty package — last resort, see e17 rep-only block.
👉 Never discount without adjusting scope first. A number that drops for no reason tells the homeowner the first number was made up.

phases.label: THE STEP-OUTSIDE
script: 👉 Situational. Primarily for appointments where both decision-makers are present and need to confer.
⏱ 5 minutes outside. No longer.
Tone/Mood: Completely relaxed. This only works if the rep genuinely doesn't seem to need the answer.
"You know what — let me get out of your hair for a few minutes.
I want to double-check a couple of the track measurements and grab some detail photos for the file anyway. Gives you two a chance to talk without me sitting here.
I'll leave everything right here — both options, the fabric book, all of it. Take your time."
👉 Leave the iPad open to the two options. Leave the samples on the table.
👉 Go outside and actually do the work.
Coming back in:
"Alright, got what I needed. So — where'd you two land?"
👉 Then stop. Do not re-pitch. Do not fill the silence.

modules.coaching_note:
The step-outside gives a couple permission to be honest with each other, which they will not do with a salesperson at the table. It also removes you as the thing being decided about — the conversation becomes about the screens, not about whether they like you.

Five minutes. Not two, not fifteen. Two isn't enough for a real conversation and fifteen lets them talk themselves out of it.

Don't use this on single-decision-maker appointments. There's nobody to confer with and it just breaks momentum.
